transcript:
00:00 Ava Chen: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, um we'll kick off. quick agenda — results review, tuning notes, next steps. 00:08 Priya Rao: thanks, ava. morning all. sorry we had a swim lane overlap with infra but we're good now. 00:14 Miguel Torres: no worries, yeah so recap from last week we ran the initial continuous batching patch on the dedicated pool and we saw throughput up ~1.8x on the 512-token profile but tail latency regressed slightly at high concurrency. 00:28 Evan Liu: correct, we also saw queuing, like when we pushed above 20 concurrent requests the queue started ballooning. 00:35 Marcus Green: can you explain the queueing behaviour again — is that the runtime or our load-balancer? 00:42 Miguel Torres: it's a mix, um the runtime's batching strategy will accumulate requests up to the batch size or until a dispatch timeout. at high concurrency, multiple dispatch windows overlap and we hit a scheduling bottleneck, plus KV cache hot-keys cause a small CPU spike on the router side. 00:58 Priya Rao: KV cache? do you mean key-value, the cache that stores prefixes? we call that prefix cache internally, might be different naming. 01:05 Miguel Torres: yeah sorry different names, KC cache/prefix cache same thing. 01:09 Ava Chen: for context our target is 200 qps steady with p95 latency <= 180ms for 256-token average, correct? Priya: is that still the success criteria? 01:20 Priya Rao: yep those are the goals. maybe for the longer prompts we tolerate higher p95. 01:26 Lina Ortiz: one constraint — our infra team wants to avoid huge concurrency changes in prod, they'd prefer queueing with backpressure rather than spinning up more instances. 01:36 Miguel Torres: that's useful, so we focus tuning on batching/concurrency and queue sizing, not autoscale. 01:41 Ava Chen: quick data dump — Miguel, can you summarise the numbers from last night's run? 01:46 Miguel Torres: sure. run A: baseline (no continuous batching) — 115 qps steady, p95 210ms. run B: continuous batching v1 (dispatch timeout 8ms) — 180 qps steady, p95 260ms. run C: continuous batching v1 + smaller dispatch (4ms) — 160 qps, p95 220ms. run D: batching v2 (adaptive with concurrency cap 24) — 195 qps, p95 240ms but with tail spikes. 02:12 Evan Liu: I can share the CSV offline but briefly, the queue depth histogram shows a long tail when concurrency > 20. so requests are waiting 80-200ms in queue sometimes. 02:24 Marcus Green: okay that explains the p95 bump. 02:27 Priya Rao: are the tail spikes correlated to model cache misses? 02:30 Miguel Torres: partially. we saw two patterns: one is cold KV/prefix cache refill for new prompt prefixes, second is the kernel scheduling when large batches hit the GPU causing higher latency for concurrent small-batch requests. 02:44 Ava Chen: interesting. so our levers are: dispatch timeout, max batch size, concurrency cap per worker, queuing policy (fifo vs priority), and routing to smaller-latency model variants. 02:54 Priya Rao: question — how risky is switching to priority queueing (e.g., customer facing requests prioritized) for us? 03:00 Miguel Torres: low risk in the runtime; complexity is around identifying request classes. but we can do a simple two-tier — interactive vs background — fairly easily. 03:09 Lina Ortiz: we'd want interactive to never wait more than 50ms in queue. can the runtime enforce that? 03:14 Miguel Torres: yes we can add a deadline-aware dispatch so interactive requests bypass dispatch timeout and get scheduled immediately up to concurrency cap; beyond that they go to a bounded priority queue. 03:26 Evan Liu: does that increase cost? if interactive bypasses batching then fewer tokens per GPU often means higher units per token. 03:33 Miguel Torres: tradeoff, yes. we can do hybrid: small interactive batch sizes (2-4) with a shorter dispatch timeout — still maintains some efficiency. 03:42 Ava Chen: on cost, Redwood Optimize suggestions from last time recommended quantize int8 on the mid-size model variant — Miguel, did you validate quality? 03:50 Miguel Torres: ran a 100-sample eval — minimal BLEU/ROUGE drift, llm eval still within thresholds for business prompts. so recommended. 03:58 Priya Rao: great — we want to avoid model quality regressions. if we change model variant for routing, we need an eval set to confirm parity. 04:06 Ava Chen: noted. action item: we'll run the eval for the int8 variant on your prod prompt set. 04:11 Miguel Torres: also did concurrency stress where we pinned 32 concurrent on two workers and observed GPU kernel preemption causing 30-60ms spikes. 04:21 Evan Liu: is that something the kernel scheduler can fix or hardware driver level? 04:25 Miguel Torres: mostly kernel scheduling — we can stagger execution by adding jitter between batch dispatches, and ensure worker threads don't all submit at the same instant. 04:34 Marcus Green: small question — do we need dedicated GPU pools for steady 200 qps or can we use shared with dedicated capacity? 04:41 Ava Chen: recommend Dedicated if predictable SLA matters; for cost-sensitive teams you can use shared hosted with Reserved capacity windows. 04:48 Priya Rao: we're leaning dedicated but want to avoid monthly commit if not necessary. maybe start shared + reserved burst windows then move to dedicated once steady. 04:58 Miguel Torres: that fits — for the POC we can emulate dedicated by isolating a node pool and pinning containers. gives production-like behavior without contract. 05:08 Ava Chen: back to tuning, Miguel what configs do you propose for the next bench? 05:12 Miguel Torres: config 1 — concurrency cap 16, dispatch timeout 6ms, max batch size 32, priority queueing off. config 2 — concurrency cap 24, dispatch timeout 4ms, max batch size 48, priority small-batch interactive enabled. config 3 — concurrency cap 32 with bounded priority queue, jittered dispatch, adaptive batch size (v2). 05:36 Priya Rao: can you include a run with int8 model variant in one of those? 05:39 Miguel Torres: yes put int8 on config 2. 05:41 Evan Liu: we'll want to run each config for at least 90 minutes to observe steady-state and warm/cold effects. 05:47 Ava Chen: Redwood will run 2-hour bursts per next step. sounds good. 05:52 Marcus Green: about monitoring — can you show us the dashboard widgets we'll need to watch? queue depth, batch size distribution, GPU utilization, p95/p99 latency, KV cache hit rate. 06:02 Miguel Torres: yes we'll share a dashboard. also traced spans so you can see where time is spent (router, batching, kernel). 06:11 Priya Rao: security question — if we route to smaller models or int8 variants, does that change data handling / logs? 06:18 Ava Chen: no change to data plane or audit logs — same compliance posture. we'll note the variant used per request in traces for audit. 06:26 Priya Rao: good. 06:28 Lina Ortiz: what about SSO/roles for toggling priority routing in prod? we'd need RBAC so only SRE can flip. 06:36 Samir Patel: we support RBAC toggles in Console; we can gate routing flags to roles. 06:41 Evan Liu: can we get a canary roll for the queueing changes? don't want a prod blast. 06:45 Miguel Torres: absolutely — we can do A/B 10% traffic to new queueing policy, monitor error/latency metrics and then ramp. 06:53 Priya Rao: perfect. 06:55 Ava Chen: ok let's capture the immediate ask — Miguel will run the three configs with int8 in config 2, 2-hour runs, share CSV + dashboard by Friday. Evan will upload prod traffic sample. schedule deep-dive for SRE specifics. 07:10 Marcus Green: any blocker on side of Redwood for running those benchmarks? 07:13 Miguel Torres: no blockers, but we may need to reserve a dedicated node pool for the 2-hour run, will confirm capacity. 07:20 Priya Rao: can you also include cost delta estimates for each config? we'd like to see cost per million tokens and per-qps. 07:28 Miguel Torres: yes we'll include cost modeling from Redwood Optimize. 07:32 Ava Chen: ok last quick questions? 07:35 Evan Liu: what about failover — if priority queue overflows do we drop or degrade? prefer degrade (route to cheaper model) rather than drop. 07:42 Miguel Torres: we can implement overflow policy: degrade -> route to smaller-model variant or return 503. default recommend degrade to preserve availability. 07:52 Priya Rao: agreed. 07:54 Ava Chen: wrap up then. we'll send meeting notes, schedule. thanks everyone. 07:59 Marcus Green: thanks all. 08:02 (call ends)

Summary:
- Continuous batching increased throughput significantly but caused p95 tail regressions at high concurrency.
- Root causes: KV/prefix cache cold misses and GPU kernel scheduling spikes when large batches coincide.
- Levers: dispatch timeout, max batch size, concurrency cap, priority/bounded queueing, jittered dispatch, and routing to int8/smaller model variants.
- Immediate plan: Redwood to run three benchmark configs (2-hour each); include int8 variant in config 2; share CSV + dashboards; customer to provide production traffic sample; schedule deep-dive for SREs.

Topics:
- Throughput vs p95 tradeoffs
- Continuous batching tuning (dispatch timeout, batch size)
- Priority queueing and bounded queues
- Kernel scheduling and jitter
- Int8 variant evaluation and cost modeling
